Tell the King I'd like a few words with him when he's free.
Naught's had, all's spent, / Where our desire is got without content: / 'Tis safer to be that which we destroy, / Than by destruction dwell in doubtful joy.
We've gained nothing and spent everything when we get what we wanted but no happiness with it. It's safer to be the one we destroyed than to destroy and live in uneasy joy.

How now, my lord, why do you keep alone, / Of sorriest fancies your companions making, / Using those thoughts which should indeed have died / With them they think on? Things without all remedy / Should be without regard: what's done is done.

What's this, my lord? Why do you keep to yourself, with only the most miserable fantasies for company, dwelling on thoughts that should have died with the people they're about? What can't be cured shouldn't be thought about. What's done is done.

We have scorch'd the snake, not kill'd it. / She'll close, and be herself; whilst our poor malice / Remains in danger of her former tooth. / But let the frame of things disjoint, / Both the worlds suffer, / Ere we will eat our meal in fear, and sleep / In the affliction of these terrible dreams / That shake us nightly. Better be with the dead, / Whom we, to gain our peace, have sent to peace, / Than on the torture of the mind to lie / In restless ecstasy. Duncan is in his grave; / After life's fitful fever he sleeps well; / Treason has done his worst: nor steel, nor poison, / Malice domestic, foreign levy, nothing / Can touch him further.

We've only wounded the snake, not killed it. She'll heal and be herself again, while our feeble attack leaves us in danger of her fangs as before. But let the whole universe fall apart, heaven and earth suffer, before we'll eat our meals in fear and sleep with these terrible dreams that shake us every night. It's better to be with the dead, whom we sent to peace to gain our own peace, than to lie on the rack of the mind in restless frenzy. Duncan is in his grave. After life's fitful fever he sleeps well. Treason has done its worst to him. Neither sword nor poison, enemies at home nor armies abroad, nothing can touch him now.
Come on, / Gently my lord, sleek o'er your rugged looks; / Be bright and jovial among your guests tonight.
Come on, my gentle lord, smooth over your troubled looks. Be bright and cheerful with your guests tonight.

So shall I, love; and so, I pray, be you. / Let your remembrance apply to Banquo; / Present him eminence, both with eye and tongue: / Unsafe the while, that we / Must lave our honours in these flattering streams, / And make our faces vizards to our hearts, / Disguising what they are.

I will, love, and please be the same. Make sure you pay attention to Banquo. Honour him with your looks and your words. We're unsafe while we have to wash our honours in these streams of flattery and make our faces masks for our hearts, hiding what they are.
O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife! / Thou know'st that Banquo, and his Fleance, lives.
Oh, my mind is full of scorpions, dear wife! You know that Banquo and his Fleance are still alive.
But in them nature's copy's not eterne.
But they don't have a lease on life for ever.

There's comfort yet; they are assailable. / Then be thou jocund. Ere the bat hath flown / His cloister'd flight, ere to black Hecate's summons / The shard-born beetle, with his drowsy hums, / Hath rung night's yawning peal, there shall be done / A deed of dreadful note.

There's comfort in that: they can be attacked. So be cheerful. Before the bat has flown its flight around the cloisters, before the beetle, born in dung, has answered black Hecate's call and rung night's sleepy bell with its drowsy humming, a deed of dreadful fame will be done.

Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck, / Till thou applaud the deed. Come, seeling night, / Scarf up the tender eye of pitiful day, / And with thy bloody and invisible hand / Cancel and tear to pieces that great bond / Which keeps me pale!—Light thickens; and the crow / Makes wing to th' rooky wood. / Good things of day begin to droop and drowse, / Whiles night's black agents to their preys do rouse. / Thou marvell'st at my words: but hold thee still; / Things bad begun make strong themselves by ill. / So, pr'ythee, go with me.

Keep yourself innocent of knowing, dearest chick, until you can applaud the deed. Come, night that sews up eyes, blindfold the tender eye of pitying day, and with your bloody, invisible hand cancel and tear to pieces the great bond of Banquo's life that keeps me pale with fear! The light is thickening, and the crow is flying to the wood full of rooks. The good creatures of the day begin to droop and doze, while night's black agents wake up to hunt their prey. You're amazed at my words, but stay calm. Things started badly grow strong through more evil. So, please, come with me.
But who did bid thee join with us?
But who told you to join us?
He needs not our mistrust; since he delivers / Our offices and what we have to do / To the direction just.
We don't need to distrust him, since he's told us our duties and what we have to do exactly as we were instructed.
Then stand with us. / The west yet glimmers with some streaks of day. / Now spurs the lated traveller apace, / To gain the timely inn; and near approaches / The subject of our watch.
Then stand with us. The west is still glimmering with a few streaks of daylight. Now the late traveller spurs his horse on to reach the inn in time, and the man we're waiting for is getting close.
[Within] Give us a light there, ho!
Then 'tis he; the rest / That are within the note of expectation / Already are i' th' court.
Then it's him. All the other expected guests are already at court.
His horses are being taken the long way round.
Almost a mile; but he does usually, / So all men do, from hence to the palace gate / Make it their walk.
Almost a mile. But he usually walks from here to the palace gate, like everyone does.
O, treachery! Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly! / Thou mayst revenge—O slave!
Oh, treachery! Run, good Fleance, run, run, run! You may get revenge. Oh, villain!
Who did strike out the light?
There's but one down: the son is fled.
Only one's down. The son has got away.
We have lost best half of our affair.
We've lost the better half of our job.
Well, let's away, and say how much is done.
Well, let's go and report how much is done.
You know your own degrees, sit down. At first / And last the hearty welcome.
You know your own ranks, so sit down accordingly. From the first to the last of you, a hearty welcome.
Ourself will mingle with society, / And play the humble host. / Our hostess keeps her state; but, in best time, / We will require her welcome.
I'll mingle with the company and play the humble host. Our hostess will stay in her chair of state, but at the right time we'll ask her to welcome you.
Pronounce it for me, sir, to all our friends; / For my heart speaks they are welcome.
Say it for me, sir, to all our friends, because my heart says they're welcome.
See, they encounter thee with their hearts' thanks. / Both sides are even: here I'll sit i' th' midst. / Be large in mirth; anon we'll drink a measure / The table round. There's blood upon thy face.

See, they answer you with their heartfelt thanks. Both sides of the table are even. I'll sit here in the middle. Enjoy yourselves freely. Soon we'll drink a toast round the table. [To the Murderer] There's blood on your face.
'Tis better thee without than he within. / Is he dispatch'd?
It's better on you outside than in him. Is he finished off?
My lord, his throat is cut. That I did for him.
My lord, his throat is cut. I did that to him.
Thou art the best o' th' cut-throats; / Yet he's good that did the like for Fleance: / If thou didst it, thou art the nonpareil.
You're the best of the cut-throats. But whoever did the same to Fleance is good too. If you did it, you have no equal.

Then comes my fit again: I had else been perfect; / Whole as the marble, founded as the rock, / As broad and general as the casing air: / But now I am cabin'd, cribb'd, confin'd, bound in / To saucy doubts and fears. But Banquo's safe?

Then my fit of fear comes back. Otherwise I'd have been perfect, as solid as marble, as firmly founded as rock, as free and unbounded as the air around us. But now I'm shut in, cramped, confined, tied up with insolent doubts and fears. But is Banquo safe?
Ay, my good lord. Safe in a ditch he bides, / With twenty trenched gashes on his head; / The least a death to nature.
Yes, my good lord. He's safe in a ditch, with twenty deep gashes in his head, the smallest of them enough to kill him.
Thanks for that. / There the grown serpent lies; the worm that's fled / Hath nature that in time will venom breed, / No teeth for th' present.—Get thee gone; tomorrow / We'll hear, ourselves, again.
Thanks for that. There lies the grown snake. The young one that's escaped has a nature that will breed poison in time, but no teeth for now. Go. Tomorrow we'll talk again.

My royal lord, / You do not give the cheer: the feast is sold / That is not often vouch'd, while 'tis a-making, / 'Tis given with welcome. To feed were best at home; / From thence the sauce to meat is ceremony; / Meeting were bare without it.

My royal lord, you're not making the guests welcome. A feast where the host doesn't keep showing that it's given with welcome is like a meal people have paid for. Eating is best done at home. Away from home, ceremony is the sauce that flavours the meat. Gatherings would be bare without it.
Sweet remembrancer!— / Now, good digestion wait on appetite, / And health on both!
Thank you for reminding me! Now, may good digestion follow a good appetite, and health follow both!
Would your Highness please sit down?
Here had we now our country's honour roof'd, / Were the grac'd person of our Banquo present; / Who may I rather challenge for unkindness / Than pity for mischance!
We'd have all the nobility of our country under one roof now, if our gracious Banquo were here. I hope I can blame him for being unkind rather than pity him for some accident!
His absence, sir, / Lays blame upon his promise. Please't your Highness / To grace us with your royal company?
His absence, sir, shows he broke his promise. Would your Highness please honour us with your royal company?
Here is a place reserv'd, sir.
Here's a place kept for you, sir.
Here, my good lord. What is't that moves your Highness?
Here, my good lord. What is it that upsets your Highness?
Which of you have done this?
Which of you has done this?
Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake / Thy gory locks at me.
You can't say I did it. Don't shake your bloody hair at me.
Gentlemen, rise; his Highness is not well.
Gentlemen, rise. His Highness isn't well.

Sit, worthy friends. My lord is often thus, / And hath been from his youth: pray you, keep seat; / The fit is momentary; upon a thought / He will again be well. If much you note him, / You shall offend him, and extend his passion. / Feed, and regard him not.—Are you a man?

Sit, worthy friends. My lord is often like this, and has been since he was young. Please, stay seated. The fit only lasts a moment. In no time he'll be well again. If you stare at him, you'll offend him and make his fit worse. Eat, and take no notice of him. [To Macbeth] Are you a man?
Ay, and a bold one, that dare look on that / Which might appal the devil.
Yes, and a brave one, who dares to look at something that would terrify the devil.

O proper stuff! / This is the very painting of your fear: / This is the air-drawn dagger which you said, / Led you to Duncan. O, these flaws, and starts / (Impostors to true fear), would well become / A woman's story at a winter's fire, / Authoris'd by her grandam. Shame itself! / Why do you make such faces? When all's done, / You look but on a stool.

What nonsense! This is just a picture painted by your fear. This is the dagger drawn in the air that you said led you to Duncan. Oh, these outbursts and jumps, which are fakes compared with real fear, would suit a woman's story by a winter fire, vouched for by her grandmother. Shame on you! Why are you making such faces? When all's said and done, you're only looking at a stool.

Pr'ythee, see there! / Behold! look! lo! how say you? / Why, what care I? If thou canst nod, speak too.— / If charnel houses and our graves must send / Those that we bury back, our monuments / Shall be the maws of kites.
Please, look there! Look! Look! What do you say? Why, what do I care? If you can nod, speak too. If burial vaults and graves send back those we bury, our tombs will be the stomachs of birds of prey.
What, has your foolishness completely unmanned you?
If I stand here, I saw him.
As sure as I'm standing here, I saw him.

Blood hath been shed ere now, i' th' olden time, / Ere humane statute purg'd the gentle weal; / Ay, and since too, murders have been perform'd / Too terrible for the ear: the time has been, / That, when the brains were out, the man would die, / And there an end; but now they rise again, / With twenty mortal murders on their crowns, / And push us from our stools. This is more strange / Than such a murder is.

Blood has been shed before now, in the old days, before humane laws cleaned up society and made it gentle. Yes, and since then too, murders have been done too terrible to hear about. There was a time when, if a man's brains were knocked out, he would die, and that was the end of it. But now they rise again, with twenty deadly wounds on their heads, and push us off our stools. This is stranger than a murder like that.
My worthy lord, / Your noble friends do lack you.
My worthy lord, your noble friends are missing you.

I do forget.— / Do not muse at me, my most worthy friends. / I have a strange infirmity, which is nothing / To those that know me. Come, love and health to all; / Then I'll sit down.—Give me some wine, fill full.— / I drink to the general joy o' th' whole table, / And to our dear friend Banquo, whom we miss: / Would he were here.

I'm forgetting. Don't wonder at me, my most worthy friends. I have a strange illness, which is nothing to those who know me. Come, love and health to all, and then I'll sit down. Give me some wine. Fill it up. I drink to the happiness of the whole table, and to our dear friend Banquo, whom we miss. I wish he were here!
To all, and him, we thirst, / And all to all.
To all, and to him, we drink, and everyone drink to everyone.
Our duty to you, and we drink your toast.
Avaunt! and quit my sight! let the earth hide thee! / Thy bones are marrowless, thy blood is cold; / Thou hast no speculation in those eyes / Which thou dost glare with!
Get away! Out of my sight! Let the earth hide you! Your bones have no marrow, your blood is cold. There's no sight in those eyes you're glaring with!
Think of this, good peers, / But as a thing of custom: 'tis no other, / Only it spoils the pleasure of the time.
Good lords, think of this only as a habit of his. It's nothing else. It just spoils the pleasure of the evening.

What man dare, I dare: / Approach thou like the rugged Russian bear, / The arm'd rhinoceros, or th' Hyrcan tiger; / Take any shape but that, and my firm nerves / Shall never tremble: or be alive again, / And dare me to the desert with thy sword; / If trembling I inhabit then, protest me / The baby of a girl. Hence, horrible shadow! / Unreal mock'ry, hence!

Whatever a man dares, I dare. Come at me like the rough Russian bear, the armoured rhinoceros or the tiger from Hyrcania. Take any shape but that, and my steady nerves will never tremble. Or come alive again and challenge me to fight you with swords in some desert. If I tremble then, call me a little girl's doll. Go, horrible shadow! Unreal mockery, go!
Why, so;—being gone, / I am a man again.—Pray you, sit still.
Why, there. Now it's gone, I'm a man again. Please, stay seated.
You have displaced the mirth, broke the good meeting / With most admir'd disorder.
You've driven away the fun and broken up the happy gathering with this astonishing disorder.

Can such things be, / And overcome us like a summer's cloud, / Without our special wonder? You make me strange / Even to the disposition that I owe, / When now I think you can behold such sights, / And keep the natural ruby of your cheeks, / When mine are blanch'd with fear.

Can such things happen and pass over us like a summer cloud without our being amazed? You make me feel a stranger to my own nature, when I think you can see such sights and keep the natural red in your cheeks, while mine are white with fear.
I pray you, speak not; he grows worse and worse; / Question enrages him. At once, good night:— / Stand not upon the order of your going, / But go at once.
Please, don't speak. He's getting worse and worse. Questions make him furious. Good night at once. Don't worry about leaving in order of rank. Just go at once.
Good night; and better health / Attend his Majesty!
Good night, and may better health come to his Majesty!
A kind good night to all!
A kind good night to all!

It will have blood, they say, blood will have blood. / Stones have been known to move, and trees to speak; / Augurs, and understood relations, have / By magot-pies, and choughs, and rooks, brought forth / The secret'st man of blood.—What is the night?

It will have blood, they say: blood will have blood. Gravestones have been known to move, and trees to speak. Omens, and signs read in the connections between things, have revealed the most secret murderer through magpies, jackdaws and rooks. What time of night is it?
Almost at odds with morning, which is which.
Almost at the point where you can't tell if it's night or morning.
How say'st thou, that Macduff denies his person / At our great bidding?
What do you say to Macduff refusing to come when I commanded him?
Did you send to him, sir?
Did you send for him, sir?

I hear it by the way; but I will send. / There's not a one of them but in his house / I keep a servant fee'd. I will tomorrow / (And betimes I will) to the Weird Sisters: / More shall they speak; for now I am bent to know, / By the worst means, the worst. For mine own good, / All causes shall give way: I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more, / Returning were as tedious as go o'er. / Strange things I have in head, that will to hand, / Which must be acted ere they may be scann'd.

I heard it indirectly, but I will send. There isn't one of them in whose house I don't keep a paid servant as a spy. Tomorrow, and early, I'll go to the Weird Sisters. They'll tell me more, because now I'm determined to know the worst, by the worst means. Everything must give way to my own good. I've waded so far into blood that if I stopped now, going back would be as hard as going on. I have strange things in my head that I'll carry out, things that must be done before they can be thought about.
You lack the season of all natures, sleep.
You lack what keeps every living thing fresh: sleep.
Come, we'll to sleep. My strange and self-abuse / Is the initiate fear that wants hard use. / We are yet but young in deed.
Come, we'll go to sleep. My strange delusion is a beginner's fear that needs hardening with practice. We're still young in deeds like this.
Why, how now, Hecate? you look angerly.
Why, what's the matter, Hecate? You look angry.

Have I not reason, beldams as you are, / Saucy and overbold? How did you dare / To trade and traffic with Macbeth / In riddles and affairs of death; / And I, the mistress of your charms, / The close contriver of all harms, / Was never call'd to bear my part, / Or show the glory of our art? / And, which is worse, all you have done / Hath been but for a wayward son, / Spiteful and wrathful; who, as others do, / Loves for his own ends, not for you. / But make amends now: get you gone, / And at the pit of Acheron / Meet me i' th' morning: thither he / Will come to know his destiny. / Your vessels and your spells provide, / Your charms, and everything beside. / I am for th' air; this night I'll spend / Unto a dismal and a fatal end. / Great business must be wrought ere noon. / Upon the corner of the moon / There hangs a vap'rous drop profound; / I'll catch it ere it come to ground: / And that, distill'd by magic sleights, / Shall raise such artificial sprites, / As, by the strength of their illusion, / Shall draw him on to his confusion. / He shall spurn fate, scorn death, and bear / His hopes 'bove wisdom, grace, and fear. / And you all know, security / Is mortals' chiefest enemy.

Haven't I got reason to be, you old hags, rude and over-bold as you are? How did you dare to trade and deal with Macbeth in riddles and matters of death, while I, the mistress of your spells, the secret planner of all harm, was never called to play my part or show the glory of our art? And what's worse, everything you've done has been for a stubborn son, spiteful and angry, who, like others, loves for his own ends, not for you. But make up for it now. Go, and meet me in the morning at the pit of Acheron. He'll come there to learn his destiny. Get your pots and spells ready, your charms and everything else. I'm off into the air. I'll spend this night working for a dreadful, deadly end. Great business must be done before noon. A heavy drop of vapour hangs on the tip of the moon. I'll catch it before it reaches the ground, and that, distilled by magic tricks, will raise such deceiving spirits that by the strength of their illusion they'll draw him on to his ruin. He'll defy fate, laugh at death and put his hopes above wisdom, goodness and fear. And you all know that overconfidence is mortals' greatest enemy.
Hark! I am call'd; my little spirit, see, / Sits in a foggy cloud and stays for me.
Listen! I'm being called. My little spirit is sitting in a foggy cloud, waiting for me.
Come, let's make haste; she'll soon be back again.
Come, let's hurry. She'll be back again soon.

My former speeches have but hit your thoughts, / Which can interpret farther: only, I say, / Thing's have been strangely borne. The gracious Duncan / Was pitied of Macbeth:—marry, he was dead:— / And the right valiant Banquo walk'd too late; / Whom, you may say, if't please you, Fleance kill'd, / For Fleance fled. Men must not walk too late. / Who cannot want the thought, how monstrous / It was for Malcolm and for Donalbain / To kill their gracious father? damned fact! / How it did grieve Macbeth! did he not straight, / In pious rage, the two delinquents tear / That were the slaves of drink and thralls of sleep? / Was not that nobly done? Ay, and wisely too; / For 'twould have anger'd any heart alive, / To hear the men deny't. So that, I say, / He has borne all things well: and I do think, / That had he Duncan's sons under his key / (As, and't please heaven, he shall not) they should find / What 'twere to kill a father; so should Fleance. / But, peace!—for from broad words, and 'cause he fail'd / His presence at the tyrant's feast, I hear, / Macduff lives in disgrace. Sir, can you tell / Where he bestows himself?

What I've said before has only matched your own thoughts, and you can draw your own conclusions. I'll only say that things have been handled strangely. The gracious Duncan was pitied by Macbeth, after he was dead, of course. And the brave Banquo walked out too late. You could say, if you like, that Fleance killed him, since Fleance ran away. Men mustn't walk out too late. Who can help thinking how monstrous it was for Malcolm and Donalbain to kill their gracious father? Damned deed! How it upset Macbeth! Didn't he immediately, in holy rage, tear apart the two offenders, who were slaves to drink and prisoners of sleep? Wasn't that nobly done? Yes, and wisely too, because it would have angered any living heart to hear the men deny it. So I'd say he has handled everything well. And I do think that if he had Duncan's sons locked up, which heaven forbid, they'd find out what it means to kill a father. And so would Fleance. But quiet! I hear that because he spoke too freely, and because he didn't come to the tyrant's feast, Macduff is in disgrace. Sir, can you tell me where he is?

The son of Duncan, / From whom this tyrant holds the due of birth, / Lives in the English court and is receiv'd / Of the most pious Edward with such grace / That the malevolence of fortune nothing / Takes from his high respect. Thither Macduff / Is gone to pray the holy king, upon his aid / To wake Northumberland, and warlike Siward / That, by the help of these (with Him above / To ratify the work), we may again / Give to our tables meat, sleep to our nights; / Free from our feasts and banquets bloody knives, / Do faithful homage, and receive free honours, / All which we pine for now. And this report / Hath so exasperate the King that he / Prepares for some attempt of war.

Duncan's son, Malcolm, whose birthright this tyrant has taken, lives at the English court, and is welcomed so graciously by the most holy King Edward that his bad luck takes nothing from the high respect he's shown. Macduff has gone there to beg the holy king to help by stirring up Northumberland and the warlike Siward, so that with their help, and God above to approve the work, we can again put food on our tables and sleep in our nights, free our feasts and banquets from bloody knives, pay true respect to a king and receive honours freely, all of which we long for now. And this news has so angered Macbeth that he's preparing for war.
He did: and with an absolute "Sir, not I," / The cloudy messenger turns me his back, / And hums, as who should say, "You'll rue the time / That clogs me with this answer."
He did. And with a flat "Not me, sir", the scowling messenger turned his back on him and muttered, as if to say, "You'll regret the time you gave me this answer."

And that well might / Advise him to a caution, t' hold what distance / His wisdom can provide. Some holy angel / Fly to the court of England, and unfold / His message ere he come, that a swift blessing / May soon return to this our suffering country / Under a hand accurs'd!

And that might well warn Macduff to be careful and keep as far away as his good sense allows. May some holy angel fly to the court of England and deliver his message before he gets there, so that a swift blessing may soon come back to our country, suffering under a cursed hand!
I'll send my prayers with him.
I'll send my prayers with him.
Thrice the brinded cat hath mew'd.
Three times the striped cat has mewed.
Thrice, and once the hedge-pig whin'd.
Three times, and once the hedgehog whined.
Harpier, my spirit, is crying, "It's time, it's time."
Round about the cauldron go; / In the poison'd entrails throw.— / Toad, that under cold stone / Days and nights has thirty-one / Swelter'd venom sleeping got, / Boil thou first i' th' charmed pot!
Go round and round the cauldron and throw in the poisoned guts. Toad, who slept under a cold stone for thirty-one days and nights, sweating out venom, you boil first in the magic pot!
Double, double, toil and trouble; / Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble.
Double, double, toil and trouble; fire, burn, and cauldron, bubble.

Fillet of a fenny snake, / In the cauldron boil and bake; / Eye of newt, and toe of frog, / Wool of bat, and tongue of dog, / Adder's fork, and blind-worm's sting, / Lizard's leg, and howlet's wing, / For a charm of powerful trouble, / Like a hell-broth boil and bubble.

Slice of a snake from the marsh, boil and bake in the cauldron. Eye of newt and toe of frog, fur of bat and tongue of dog, forked tongue of an adder and sting of a slow-worm, leg of a lizard and wing of an owlet, for a spell of powerful trouble, boil and bubble like a broth from hell.
Double, double, toil and trouble; / Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble.
Double, double, toil and trouble; fire, burn, and cauldron, bubble.

Scale of dragon, tooth of wolf, / Witch's mummy, maw and gulf / Of the ravin'd salt-sea shark, / Root of hemlock digg'd i' th' dark, / Liver of blaspheming Jew, / Gall of goat, and slips of yew / Sliver'd in the moon's eclipse, / Nose of Turk, and Tartar's lips, / Finger of birth-strangled babe / Ditch-deliver'd by a drab, / Make the gruel thick and slab: / Add thereto a tiger's chaudron, / For th' ingredients of our cauldron.

Scale of dragon, tooth of wolf, a witch's mummified flesh, the stomach and gullet of the ravenous salt-sea shark, a hemlock root dug up in the dark, the liver of a Jew who blasphemed, the bile of a goat and cuttings of yew sliced off during an eclipse of the moon, the nose of a Turk and lips of a Tartar, the finger of a baby strangled at birth, delivered in a ditch by a prostitute: make the stew thick and sticky. Add a tiger's guts as well, to the ingredients of our cauldron.
Double, double, toil and trouble; / Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble.
Double, double, toil and trouble; fire, burn, and cauldron, bubble.
Cool it with a baboon's blood. / Then the charm is firm and good.
Cool it with a baboon's blood. Then the spell is firm and good.
O, well done! I commend your pains, / And everyone shall share i' th' gains. / And now about the cauldron sing, / Like elves and fairies in a ring, / Enchanting all that you put in.
Oh, well done! I praise your work, and everyone will share in the profits. And now sing around the cauldron, like elves and fairies in a ring, putting a spell on everything you've put in.
By the pricking of my thumbs, / Something wicked this way comes. / Open, locks, / Whoever knocks!
By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked is coming this way. Open, locks, whoever's knocking!
How now, you secret, black, and midnight hags! / What is't you do?
Well, you secret, black, midnight hags! What are you doing?

I conjure you, by that which you profess, / (Howe'er you come to know it) answer me: / Though you untie the winds, and let them fight / Against the churches; though the yesty waves / Confound and swallow navigation up; / Though bladed corn be lodg'd, and trees blown down; / Though castles topple on their warders' heads; / Though palaces and pyramids do slope / Their heads to their foundations; though the treasure / Of nature's germens tumble all together, / Even till destruction sicken, answer me / To what I ask you.

I call on you, by the black art you practise, however you came to know it, answer me. Even if you untie the winds and let them fight against the churches, even if the foaming waves wreck and swallow up all ships, even if the ripe corn is flattened and trees blown down, even if castles topple onto their guards' heads, even if palaces and pyramids bend their tops down to their foundations, even if all the seeds that nature creates from tumble together, until destruction itself is sick of destroying, answer what I ask you.
Say, if thou'dst rather hear it from our mouths, / Or from our masters?
Tell us, would you rather hear it from our mouths, or from our masters'?
Call them. Let me see them.
Pour in sow's blood, that hath eaten / Her nine farrow; grease that's sweaten / From the murderer's gibbet throw / Into the flame.
Pour in the blood of a sow that has eaten her nine piglets, and throw into the flame the grease that's sweated from a murderer's gallows.
Come, high or low; / Thyself and office deftly show!
Come, high or low spirit, show yourself and what you do with skill!
He knows thy thought: / Hear his speech, but say thou naught.
He knows what you're thinking. Hear what he says, but say nothing.
Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth! Beware Macduff; / Beware the Thane of Fife.—Dismiss me.—Enough.
Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth! Beware Macduff. Beware the Thane of Fife. Let me go. Enough.
Whate'er thou art, for thy good caution, thanks; / Thou hast harp'd my fear aright.—But one word more.
Whatever you are, thanks for your good warning. You've struck exactly on my fear. But one word more...
He will not be commanded. Here's another, / More potent than the first.
He won't be ordered. Here's another, more powerful than the first.
Had I three ears, I'd hear thee.
If I had three ears, I'd listen to you with all of them.
Be bloody, bold, and resolute. Laugh to scorn / The power of man, for none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth.
Be bloody, bold and determined. Laugh at the power of man, because no one born of a woman will harm Macbeth.

Then live, Macduff: what need I fear of thee? / But yet I'll make assurance double sure, / And take a bond of fate. Thou shalt not live; / That I may tell pale-hearted fear it lies, / And sleep in spite of thunder.

Then live, Macduff. Why do I need to fear you? But still, I'll make doubly sure, and take a guarantee from fate. You won't live, so that I can tell my cowardly fear that it's lying, and sleep in spite of thunder.
What is this, / That rises like the issue of a king, / And wears upon his baby brow the round / And top of sovereignty?
What is this, that rises like the child of a king, and wears the round crown of royalty on his baby forehead?
Listen, but don't speak to it.

Be lion-mettled, proud, and take no care / Who chafes, who frets, or where conspirers are: / Macbeth shall never vanquish'd be, until / Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill / Shall come against him.
Be as brave as a lion, proud, and don't care who rages, who complains, or where plotters are. Macbeth will never be defeated until Great Birnam Wood comes to fight him on high Dunsinane Hill.

That will never be: / Who can impress the forest; bid the tree / Unfix his earth-bound root? Sweet bodements, good! / Rebellious head, rise never till the wood / Of Birnam rise, and our high-plac'd Macbeth / Shall live the lease of nature, pay his breath / To time and mortal custom.—Yet my heart / Throbs to know one thing: tell me, if your art / Can tell so much, shall Banquo's issue ever / Reign in this kingdom?

That will never happen. Who can force the forest into his army, or order a tree to pull up its root from the earth? Sweet prophecies! Good! Rebellion, never raise your head until Birnam Wood rises, and Macbeth, in his high place, will live out his natural life and give up his last breath to time and death like everyone. But my heart is throbbing to know one thing. Tell me, if your art can tell so much: will Banquo's children ever reign in this kingdom?
Don't try to know any more.
I will be satisfied: deny me this, / And an eternal curse fall on you! Let me know. / Why sinks that cauldron? and what noise is this?
I will have an answer. If you refuse me this, may an eternal curse fall on you! Let me know. Why is that cauldron sinking? And what's that noise?
Show his eyes, and grieve his heart; / Come like shadows, so depart!
Show his eyes and grieve his heart. Come like shadows, and leave the same way!

Thou are too like the spirit of Banquo. Down! / Thy crown does sear mine eyeballs:—and thy hair, / Thou other gold-bound brow, is like the first. / A third is like the former.—Filthy hags! / Why do you show me this?—A fourth!—Start, eyes! / What, will the line stretch out to th' crack of doom? / Another yet!—A seventh!—I'll see no more:— / And yet the eighth appears, who bears a glass / Which shows me many more; and some I see / That twofold balls and treble sceptres carry. / Horrible sight!—Now I see 'tis true; / For the blood-bolter'd Banquo smiles upon me, / And points at them for his.—What! is this so?

You're too much like Banquo's ghost. Down! Your crown burns my eyeballs. And your hair, you second forehead bound with gold, is like the first. A third is like the one before. Filthy hags! Why are you showing me this? A fourth! Eyes, jump out of my head! What, will the line go on till the end of the world? Another! A seventh! I won't look any more. And yet the eighth appears, holding a mirror that shows me many more, and I see some carrying two orbs and three sceptres. Horrible sight! Now I see it's true, because Banquo, his hair matted with blood, is smiling at me and pointing at them as his descendants. What! Is this true?

Ay, sir, all this is so:—but why / Stands Macbeth thus amazedly?— / Come, sisters, cheer we up his sprites, / And show the best of our delights. / I'll charm the air to give a sound, / While you perform your antic round; / That this great king may kindly say, / Our duties did his welcome pay.

Yes, sir, all this is true. But why is Macbeth standing there so amazed? Come, sisters, let's cheer up his spirits and show him our best entertainment. I'll put a spell on the air to make music while you do your wild dance in a ring, so that this great king may kindly say we paid him the welcome he deserved.
Where are they? Gone?—Let this pernicious hour / Stand aye accursed in the calendar!— / Come in, without there!
Where are they? Gone? Let this deadly hour be cursed in the calendar for ever! You out there, come in!
Did you see the Weird Sisters?
Infected be the air whereon they ride; / And damn'd all those that trust them!—I did hear / The galloping of horse: who was't came by?
May the air they ride on be infected, and damned be all who trust them! I heard horses galloping. Who was it that came by?
'Tis two or three, my lord, that bring you word / Macduff is fled to England.
It's two or three men, my lord, bringing you news that Macduff has fled to England.

Time, thou anticipat'st my dread exploits: / The flighty purpose never is o'ertook / Unless the deed go with it. From this moment / The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand. And even now, / To crown my thoughts with acts, be it thought and done: / The castle of Macduff I will surprise; / Seize upon Fife; give to th' edge o' th' sword / His wife, his babes, and all unfortunate souls / That trace him in his line. No boasting like a fool; / This deed I'll do before this purpose cool: / But no more sights!—Where are these gentlemen? / Come, bring me where they are.

Time, you've got ahead of my dreadful plans. A fleeting purpose is never carried out unless the deed goes with it at once. From this moment, the first thoughts of my heart will be the first acts of my hand. And right now, to crown my thoughts with action, let it be thought and done. I'll attack Macduff's castle without warning, seize Fife, and put to the sword his wife, his children and all the unlucky souls of his family. No boasting like a fool. I'll do this deed before my purpose cools. But no more visions! Where are these gentlemen? Come, take me to them.
What had he done, to make him fly the land?
What had he done, to make him run away from the country?
He had none: / His flight was madness: when our actions do not, / Our fears do make us traitors.
He had no patience. His running away was madness. Even when our actions don't make us traitors, our fears do.
You know not / Whether it was his wisdom or his fear.
You don't know whether it was his wisdom or his fear.

Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes, / His mansion, and his titles, in a place / From whence himself does fly? He loves us not: / He wants the natural touch; for the poor wren, / The most diminutive of birds, will fight, / Her young ones in her nest, against the owl. / All is the fear, and nothing is the love; / As little is the wisdom, where the flight / So runs against all reason.

Wisdom! To leave his wife, to leave his children, his home and his titles in a place he runs away from himself? He doesn't love us. He lacks natural feeling. Even the poor wren, the tiniest of birds, will fight the owl to protect her young in the nest. It's all fear and no love, and there's just as little wisdom, when running away goes so much against all reason.

My dearest coz, / I pray you, school yourself: but, for your husband, / He is noble, wise, judicious, and best knows / The fits o' th' season. I dare not speak much further: / But cruel are the times, when we are traitors, / And do not know ourselves; when we hold rumour / From what we fear, yet know not what we fear, / But float upon a wild and violent sea / Each way and move—I take my leave of you: / Shall not be long but I'll be here again. / Things at the worst will cease, or else climb upward / To what they were before.—My pretty cousin, / Blessing upon you!

My dearest cousin, please, control yourself. As for your husband, he is noble, wise, sensible, and knows best the troubles of these times. I don't dare say much more. But the times are cruel when we're called traitors without knowing it ourselves, when we believe rumours because of what we fear, but don't know what we fear, and just float on a wild and violent sea, tossed every way. I'll take my leave of you. It won't be long before I'm here again. When things are at their worst they'll stop, or else climb back up to what they were before. My pretty little cousin, bless you!
Father'd he is, and yet he's fatherless.
He has a father, and yet he's fatherless.
I am so much a fool, should I stay longer, / It would be my disgrace and your discomfort: / I take my leave at once.
I'm such a fool that if I stayed longer I'd disgrace myself by crying and upset you. I'll leave at once.
Sirrah, your father's dead. / And what will you do now? How will you live?
Young man, your father's dead. And what will you do now? How will you live?
With what I get, I mean; and so do they.
On whatever I can get, I mean, and so do they.
Poor bird! thou'dst never fear the net nor lime, / The pit-fall nor the gin.
Poor bird! You'd never be afraid of the net or the bird-lime, the trap or the snare.
Why should I, mother? Poor birds they are not set for. / My father is not dead, for all your saying.
Why should I, mother? They're not set for poor birds. My father isn't dead, whatever you say.
Yes, he is dead: how wilt thou do for a father?
Yes, he's dead. What will you do for a father?
Nay, how will you do for a husband?
Well, what will you do for a husband?
Why, I can buy me twenty at any market.
Why, I can buy myself twenty at any market.
Then you'll buy 'em to sell again.
Then you'll buy them to sell again.
Thou speak'st with all thy wit; / And yet, i' faith, with wit enough for thee.
You talk with all your cleverness, and yet, really, it's clever enough for someone your age.
Was my father a traitor, mother?
Was my father a traitor, mother?
Why, one that swears and lies.
Why, someone who swears an oath and breaks it.
And be all traitors that do so?
And is everyone who does that a traitor?
Every one that does so is a traitor, and must be hanged.
Everyone who does that is a traitor, and must be hanged.
And must they all be hanged that swear and lie?
And must everyone who swears and lies be hanged?
Then the liars and swearers are fools: for there are liars and swearers / enow to beat the honest men and hang up them.
Then the liars and swearers are fools, because there are enough liars and swearers to beat the honest men and hang them.
Now, God help thee, poor monkey! But how wilt thou do for a father?
Now, God help you, you poor little monkey! But what will you do for a father?
If he were dead, you'ld weep for him: if you would not, it were a good / sign that I should quickly have a new father.
If he were dead, you'd cry for him. If you didn't, it would be a good sign that I'd soon have a new father.
Poor little chatterbox, how you talk!

Bless you, fair dame! I am not to you known, / Though in your state of honour I am perfect. / I doubt some danger does approach you nearly: / If you will take a homely man's advice, / Be not found here; hence, with your little ones. / To fright you thus, methinks, I am too savage; / To do worse to you were fell cruelty, / Which is too nigh your person. Heaven preserve you! / I dare abide no longer.

Bless you, good lady! You don't know me, though I know well your noble rank. I'm afraid some danger is coming close to you. If you'll take a plain man's advice, don't be found here. Go, with your little ones. I feel I'm too savage to frighten you like this. But to do worse to you would be terrible cruelty, and that's coming too close to you. Heaven protect you! I don't dare stay any longer.

Whither should I fly? / I have done no harm. But I remember now / I am in this earthly world, where to do harm / Is often laudable; to do good sometime / Accounted dangerous folly: why then, alas, / Do I put up that womanly defence, / To say I have done no harm? What are these faces?

Where should I run to? I've done no harm. But I remember now that I'm in this earthly world, where doing harm is often praised and doing good is sometimes thought to be dangerous foolishness. Why then, alas, do I put up that womanly defence of saying I've done no harm? Who are these men?
I hope, in no place so unsanctified / Where such as thou mayst find him.
I hope he's in no place so unholy that someone like you could find him.
He has kill'd me, mother: / Run away, I pray you!
He's killed me, mother. Run away, please!
Let us seek out some desolate shade and there / Weep our sad bosoms empty.
Let's find some lonely shade and cry until our sad hearts are empty.

Let us rather / Hold fast the mortal sword, and, like good men, / Bestride our down-fall'n birthdom. Each new morn / New widows howl, new orphans cry; new sorrows / Strike heaven on the face, that it resounds / As if it felt with Scotland, and yell'd out / Like syllable of dolour.

Let's rather hold tight to the deadly sword and, like good men, stand over our fallen homeland to defend it. Every new morning new widows howl and new orphans cry, and new sorrows strike heaven in the face so that it echoes as if it felt for Scotland and cried out the same sounds of pain.

What I believe, I'll wail; / What know, believe; and what I can redress, / As I shall find the time to friend, I will. / What you have spoke, it may be so, perchance. / This tyrant, whose sole name blisters our tongues, / Was once thought honest: you have loved him well; / He hath not touch'd you yet. I am young; but something / You may deserve of him through me; and wisdom / To offer up a weak, poor, innocent lamb / To appease an angry god.

I'll weep for what I believe, and I'll believe what I know, and what I can put right, when the time is on my side, I will. What you've said may perhaps be true. This tyrant, whose name alone blisters our tongues, was once thought honest. You loved him well. He hasn't harmed you yet. I'm young, but you might win something from him by betraying me, and it might be wise to sacrifice a weak, poor, innocent lamb to calm an angry god.

But Macbeth is. / A good and virtuous nature may recoil / In an imperial charge. But I shall crave your pardon. / That which you are, my thoughts cannot transpose. / Angels are bright still, though the brightest fell: / Though all things foul would wear the brows of grace, / Yet grace must still look so.

But Macbeth is. A good and virtuous nature may give way under a king's command. But I beg your pardon. My thoughts can't change what you are. Angels are still bright, though the brightest, Lucifer, fell. Even if every foul thing put on the face of goodness, goodness would still have to look like that.

Perchance even there where I did find my doubts. / Why in that rawness left you wife and child, / Those precious motives, those strong knots of love, / Without leave-taking?—I pray you, / Let not my jealousies be your dishonours, / But mine own safeties. You may be rightly just, / Whatever I shall think.

Perhaps in the very place where I found my doubts. Why did you leave your wife and child so unprotected, those precious reasons to stay, those strong ties of love, without even saying goodbye? Please, don't take my suspicions as insults to your honour. They're only to protect me. You may be completely honest, whatever I think.

Bleed, bleed, poor country! / Great tyranny, lay thou thy basis sure, / For goodness dare not check thee! wear thou thy wrongs; / The title is affeer'd.—Fare thee well, lord: / I would not be the villain that thou think'st / For the whole space that's in the tyrant's grasp / And the rich East to boot.

Bleed, bleed, poor country! Great tyranny, build your foundations firmly, because goodness doesn't dare stop you! Wear your stolen honours. Your right to them is confirmed. Farewell, lord. I wouldn't be the villain you think I am for all the land in the tyrant's grip, and all the riches of the East as well.

Be not offended: / I speak not as in absolute fear of you. / I think our country sinks beneath the yoke; / It weeps, it bleeds; and each new day a gash / Is added to her wounds. I think, withal, / There would be hands uplifted in my right; / And here, from gracious England, have I offer / Of goodly thousands: but, for all this, / When I shall tread upon the tyrant's head, / Or wear it on my sword, yet my poor country / Shall have more vices than it had before, / More suffer, and more sundry ways than ever, / By him that shall succeed.

Don't be offended. I'm not speaking out of complete distrust of you. I think our country is sinking under the yoke. It weeps, it bleeds, and each new day another gash is added to her wounds. I think, too, that hands would be raised to fight for my right, and here gracious England has offered me many thousands of men. But for all that, when I tread on the tyrant's head or carry it on my sword, my poor country will have more vices than it had before, and suffer more, and in more ways than ever, under the man who comes after him.

It is myself I mean; in whom I know / All the particulars of vice so grafted / That, when they shall be open'd, black Macbeth / Will seem as pure as snow; and the poor state / Esteem him as a lamb, being compar'd / With my confineless harms.

I mean myself. I know that every kind of vice is so rooted in me that when they are revealed, black Macbeth will seem as pure as snow, and the poor country will think him a lamb compared with my endless evils.
Not in the legions / Of horrid hell can come a devil more damn'd / In evils to top Macbeth.
Not even in the armies of horrible hell could there be a devil more damned in evil than Macbeth.

I grant him bloody, / Luxurious, avaricious, false, deceitful, / Sudden, malicious, smacking of every sin / That has a name: but there's no bottom, none, / In my voluptuousness: your wives, your daughters, / Your matrons, and your maids, could not fill up / The cistern of my lust; and my desire / All continent impediments would o'erbear, / That did oppose my will: better Macbeth / Than such an one to reign.

I admit he's bloody, lustful, greedy, false, deceitful, violent, malicious, tainted with every sin that has a name. But there's no bottom, none, to my lust. Your wives, your daughters, your married women and your young girls couldn't fill the tank of my desire, and my lust would trample every obstacle of self-control that stood in its way. It's better that Macbeth should reign than someone like me.

Boundless intemperance / In nature is a tyranny; it hath been / Th' untimely emptying of the happy throne, / And fall of many kings. But fear not yet / To take upon you what is yours: you may / Convey your pleasures in a spacious plenty, / And yet seem cold—the time you may so hoodwink. / We have willing dames enough; there cannot be / That vulture in you, to devour so many / As will to greatness dedicate themselves, / Finding it so inclin'd.

Unlimited appetite is a tyranny in a man's nature. It has emptied the happy throne before its time and brought down many kings. But don't be afraid yet to take what's yours. You can enjoy your pleasures in secret, and plenty of them, and still seem chaste. You can fool the world like that. There are enough willing women. There can't be such a vulture in you that you'd devour as many as would offer themselves to a great man, once they found he was that way inclined.

With this there grows / In my most ill-compos'd affection such / A staunchless avarice, that, were I king, / I should cut off the nobles for their lands; / Desire his jewels, and this other's house: / And my more-having would be as a sauce / To make me hunger more; that I should forge / Quarrels unjust against the good and loyal, / Destroying them for wealth.

As well as this, there grows in my wicked nature such endless greed that if I were king I'd kill the nobles for their lands, wanting this man's jewels and that man's house. And having more would only be a sauce to make me hungrier, so that I'd invent unjust quarrels with good and loyal men and destroy them for their wealth.

This avarice / Sticks deeper; grows with more pernicious root / Than summer-seeming lust; and it hath been / The sword of our slain kings: yet do not fear; / Scotland hath foisons to fill up your will, / Of your mere own. All these are portable, / With other graces weigh'd.

This greed goes deeper and grows from a more poisonous root than lust, which passes like summer. It has been the sword that killed our kings. But don't be afraid. Scotland has plenty of riches to satisfy your desire from your own royal property. All these faults can be put up with, if they're weighed against your other virtues.

But I have none: the king-becoming graces, / As justice, verity, temp'rance, stableness, / Bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, / Devotion, patience, courage, fortitude, / I have no relish of them; but abound / In the division of each several crime, / Acting it many ways. Nay, had I power, I should / Pour the sweet milk of concord into hell, / Uproar the universal peace, confound / All unity on earth.

But I have none. The virtues that suit a king, like justice, truth, self-control, steadiness, generosity, perseverance, mercy, humility, devotion, patience, courage and strength, I have no taste for them. Instead I'm full of every variety of each crime, committing it in many ways. No, if I had the power, I'd pour the sweet milk of harmony into hell, throw universal peace into uproar and destroy all unity on earth.
If such a one be fit to govern, speak: / I am as I have spoken.
If someone like that is fit to govern, say so. I am what I've said.

Fit to govern? / No, not to live.—O nation miserable, / With an untitled tyrant bloody-scepter'd, / When shalt thou see thy wholesome days again, / Since that the truest issue of thy throne / By his own interdiction stands accus'd, / And does blaspheme his breed? Thy royal father / Was a most sainted king. The queen that bore thee, / Oft'ner upon her knees than on her feet, / Died every day she lived. Fare thee well! / These evils thou repeat'st upon thyself / Have banish'd me from Scotland.—O my breast, / Thy hope ends here!

Fit to govern? No, not fit to live! O miserable nation, with a bloody tyrant holding the sceptre with no right to it, when will you see healthy days again, since the truest heir to your throne condemns himself by his own words and slanders his family? Your royal father was a most saintly king. The queen who gave birth to you, more often on her knees in prayer than on her feet, lived every day as if preparing to die. Farewell! These evils you accuse yourself of have banished me from Scotland. O my heart, your hope ends here!

Macduff, this noble passion, / Child of integrity, hath from my soul / Wiped the black scruples, reconcil'd my thoughts / To thy good truth and honour. Devilish Macbeth / By many of these trains hath sought to win me / Into his power, and modest wisdom plucks me / From over-credulous haste: but God above / Deal between thee and me! for even now / I put myself to thy direction, and / Unspeak mine own detraction; here abjure / The taints and blames I laid upon myself, / For strangers to my nature. I am yet / Unknown to woman; never was forsworn; / Scarcely have coveted what was mine own; / At no time broke my faith; would not betray / The devil to his fellow; and delight / No less in truth than life: my first false speaking / Was this upon myself. What I am truly, / Is thine and my poor country's to command: / Whither, indeed, before thy here-approach, / Old Siward, with ten thousand warlike men, / Already at a point, was setting forth. / Now we'll together, and the chance of goodness / Be like our warranted quarrel. Why are you silent?

Macduff, this noble passion, born of your honesty, has wiped the black suspicions from my soul and made my thoughts agree with your truth and honour. Devilish Macbeth has tried with many tricks like this to lure me into his power, and careful wisdom holds me back from trusting too quickly. But may God above judge between you and me! Because right now I put myself under your guidance and take back what I said against myself. I here deny the stains and faults I accused myself of, as foreign to my nature. I have never slept with a woman, never broken an oath, hardly even wanted what was mine already. I have never broken my word, wouldn't betray the devil to another devil, and love truth no less than life. The first lie I ever told was this one about myself. What I truly am is yours and my poor country's to command. In fact, before you arrived, old Siward, with ten thousand soldiers ready for war, was already setting out there. Now we'll go together, and may our chance of success be as good as our just cause! Why are you silent?
Such welcome and unwelcome things at once / 'Tis hard to reconcile.
It's hard to make sense of such welcome and unwelcome things at once.
Well; more anon.—Comes the King forth, I pray you?
Well, more later. Is the King coming out, please?

Ay, sir. There are a crew of wretched souls / That stay his cure: their malady convinces / The great assay of art; but at his touch, / Such sanctity hath heaven given his hand, / They presently amend.

Yes, sir. There's a crowd of wretched people waiting for him to cure them. Their illness defeats the greatest efforts of medicine, but heaven has given his hand such holiness that they get better as soon as he touches them.

'Tis call'd the evil: / A most miraculous work in this good king; / Which often, since my here-remain in England, / I have seen him do. How he solicits heaven, / Himself best knows, but strangely-visited people, / All swoln and ulcerous, pitiful to the eye, / The mere despair of surgery, he cures; / Hanging a golden stamp about their necks, / Put on with holy prayers: and 'tis spoken, / To the succeeding royalty he leaves / The healing benediction. With this strange virtue, / He hath a heavenly gift of prophecy; / And sundry blessings hang about his throne, / That speak him full of grace.

It's called the evil. It's a miraculous work that this good king does, which I've often seen him do since I've been in England. How he calls on heaven, he knows best himself, but he cures people strangely afflicted, all swollen and covered in ulcers, pitiful to look at, beyond all hope of surgery, by hanging a gold coin around their necks with holy prayers. And they say he will pass on this blessing of healing to the kings who come after him. As well as this strange power, he has a heavenly gift of prophecy, and many blessings surround his throne that show he is full of grace.
My countryman; but yet I know him not.
A Scotsman, but I don't know him yet.
My always gentle cousin, welcome here.
I know him now. Good God, betimes remove / The means that makes us strangers!
I know him now. Good God, soon remove what keeps us strangers!

Alas, poor country, / Almost afraid to know itself! It cannot / Be call'd our mother, but our grave, where nothing, / But who knows nothing, is once seen to smile; / Where sighs, and groans, and shrieks, that rent the air, / Are made, not mark'd; where violent sorrow seems / A modern ecstasy. The dead man's knell / Is there scarce ask'd for who; and good men's lives / Expire before the flowers in their caps, / Dying or ere they sicken.

Oh, poor country, almost afraid to know itself! It can't be called our mother, only our grave, where no one is ever seen to smile except those who know nothing, where sighs and groans and shrieks that tear the air are made but not noticed, where violent grief seems an everyday feeling. When the funeral bell rings, hardly anyone asks who it's for, and good men's lives end before the flowers in their caps wither, dying before they even fall sick.
O, relation / Too nice, and yet too true!
Oh, a report too exact, and yet too true!
That of an hour's age doth hiss the speaker; / Each minute teems a new one.
News an hour old gets the speaker hissed for being out of date. Every minute gives birth to a new one.
The tyrant has not batter'd at their peace?
The tyrant hasn't attacked their peace?
No; they were well at peace when I did leave 'em.
No, they were at peace when I left them.
Be not a niggard of your speech: how goes't?
Don't be so mean with your words. How are things?

When I came hither to transport the tidings, / Which I have heavily borne, there ran a rumour / Of many worthy fellows that were out; / Which was to my belief witness'd the rather, / For that I saw the tyrant's power afoot. / Now is the time of help. Your eye in Scotland / Would create soldiers, make our women fight, / To doff their dire distresses.

When I came here to bring the news I've been carrying so sadly, there was a rumour that many good men had risen up in arms. I believed it all the more because I saw the tyrant's army on the move. Now is the time to help. If you were seen in Scotland, it would create soldiers and make even our women fight to throw off their terrible suffering.
Be't their comfort / We are coming thither. Gracious England hath / Lent us good Siward and ten thousand men; / An older and a better soldier none / That Christendom gives out.
Let it comfort them that we're coming. Gracious England has lent us good Siward and ten thousand men. There's no older or better soldier in the Christian world.
Would I could answer / This comfort with the like! But I have words / That would be howl'd out in the desert air, / Where hearing should not latch them.
I wish I could answer this comfort with the same! But I have words that should be howled out in the empty desert air, where no ear could catch them.
What concern they? / The general cause? or is it a fee-grief / Due to some single breast?
What are they about? The general cause? Or is it a private grief belonging to one person?
No mind that's honest / But in it shares some woe, though the main part / Pertains to you alone.
There's no honest mind that doesn't share some of the sorrow, though the main part belongs to you alone.
If it be mine, / Keep it not from me, quickly let me have it.
If it's mine, don't keep it from me. Let me have it quickly.
Let not your ears despise my tongue for ever, / Which shall possess them with the heaviest sound / That ever yet they heard.
Don't let your ears hate my tongue for ever, when it fills them with the heaviest sound they've ever heard.
Your castle is surpris'd; your wife and babes / Savagely slaughter'd. To relate the manner / Were, on the quarry of these murder'd deer, / To add the death of you.
Your castle was attacked without warning, and your wife and children savagely slaughtered. To tell you how would add your death to the pile of these murdered deer.
Merciful heaven!— / What, man! ne'er pull your hat upon your brows. / Give sorrow words. The grief that does not speak / Whispers the o'er-fraught heart, and bids it break.
Merciful heaven! What, man! Don't pull your hat down over your eyes. Put your sorrow into words. Grief that doesn't speak whispers to the overloaded heart and tells it to break.
Wife, children, servants, all / That could be found.
Wife, children, servants, everyone who could be found.
And I must be from thence! / My wife kill'd too?
And I had to be away! My wife killed too?
Be comforted: / Let's make us med'cines of our great revenge, / To cure this deadly grief.
Take comfort. Let's make medicine out of our great revenge to cure this deadly grief.
He has no children.—All my pretty ones? / Did you say all?—O hell-kite!—All? / What, all my pretty chickens and their dam / At one fell swoop?
He has no children. All my pretty little ones? Did you say all? Oh, hell-hawk! All? What, all my pretty chicks and their mother in one savage swoop?

I shall do so; / But I must also feel it as a man: / I cannot but remember such things were, / That were most precious to me.—Did heaven look on, / And would not take their part? Sinful Macduff, / They were all struck for thee! Naught that I am, / Not for their own demerits, but for mine, / Fell slaughter on their souls: heaven rest them now!

I will. But I must also feel it like a man. I can't help remembering that such things existed and were the most precious things in the world to me. Did heaven watch and not take their side? Sinful Macduff, they were all struck down because of you! Wicked as I am, it wasn't for their own faults but for mine that slaughter fell on their souls. May heaven give them rest now!
Be this the whetstone of your sword. Let grief / Convert to anger; blunt not the heart, enrage it.
Let this be the stone that sharpens your sword. Let grief turn into anger. Don't dull your heart. Enrage it.

O, I could play the woman with mine eyes, / And braggart with my tongue!—But, gentle heavens, / Cut short all intermission; front to front, / Bring thou this fiend of Scotland and myself; / Within my sword's length set him; if he 'scape, / Heaven forgive him too!

Oh, I could cry like a woman and boast with my tongue! But, gentle heavens, cut out all delay. Bring this devil of Scotland and me face to face. Put him within reach of my sword. If he escapes, may heaven forgive him too!

This tune goes manly. / Come, go we to the King. Our power is ready; / Our lack is nothing but our leave. Macbeth / Is ripe for shaking, and the powers above / Put on their instruments. Receive what cheer you may; / The night is long that never finds the day.

Now you sound like a man. Come, let's go to the King. Our army is ready. All we need is to take our leave. Macbeth is ripe for shaking from the tree, and the powers above are taking up their weapons. Take what comfort you can. The night is long that never finds the day.
I have two nights watched with you, but can perceive no truth in your / report. When was it she last walked?
I've watched with you for two nights, but I can't see any truth in what you told me. When was the last time she walked?

Since his Majesty went into the field, I have seen her rise from her / bed, throw her nightgown upon her, unlock her closet, take forth paper, / fold it, write upon't, read it, afterwards seal it, and again return to / bed; yet all this while in a most fast sleep.

Since his Majesty went off to war, I've seen her get out of bed, throw on her nightgown, unlock her cabinet, take out paper, fold it, write on it, read it, then seal it and go back to bed, and all this time fast asleep.

A great perturbation in nature, to receive at once the benefit of / sleep, and do the effects of watching. In this slumbery agitation, / besides her walking and other actual performances, what, at any time, / have you heard her say?
It's a great disorder of nature to get the benefit of sleep and act as if awake at the same time. In this sleeping agitation, apart from her walking and other actions, what have you heard her say?
That, sir, which I will not report after her.
Things, sir, that I won't repeat.
You may to me; and 'tis most meet you should.
You can tell me, and it's right that you should.
Neither to you nor anyone; having no witness to confirm my speech.
Not to you or anyone, since I have no witness to back up what I say.
Lo you, here she comes! This is her very guise; and, upon my life, fast / asleep. Observe her; stand close.
Look, here she comes! This is exactly how she does it, and, on my life, fast asleep. Watch her. Keep hidden.
How came she by that light?
How did she get that candle?
Why, it stood by her: she has light by her continually; 'tis her / command.
Why, it was by her bed. She has a light by her all the time. It's her order.
You see, her eyes are open.
You see, her eyes are open.
Ay, but their sense are shut.
What is it she does now? Look how she rubs her hands.
What's she doing now? Look how she's rubbing her hands.
It is an accustomed action with her, to seem thus washing her hands. I / have known her continue in this a quarter of an hour.
It's a habit of hers, to look as if she's washing her hands. I've seen her keep this up for a quarter of an hour.
Hark, she speaks. I will set down what comes from her, to satisfy my / remembrance the more strongly.
Listen, she's speaking. I'll write down what she says, to back up my memory.

Out, damned spot! out, I say! One; two. Why, then 'tis time to do't. / Hell is murky! Fie, my lord, fie! a soldier, and afeard? What need we / fear who knows it, when none can call our power to account? Yet who / would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?

Out, damned spot! Out, I say! One, two. Why, then it's time to do it. Hell is murky! Shame, my lord, shame! A soldier, and afraid? Why should we fear who knows it, when no one can call our power to account? But who would have thought the old man had so much blood in him?
The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now?—What, will these hands / ne'er be clean? No more o' that, my lord, no more o' that: you mar all / with this starting.
The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now? What, will these hands never be clean? No more of that, my lord, no more of that. You'll ruin everything with these fits of nerves.
Go to, go to. You have known what you should not.
Well, well. You've learned things you shouldn't have.
She has spoke what she should not, I am sure of that: heaven knows what / she has known.
She's said things she shouldn't have, I'm sure of that. Heaven knows what she knows.
Here's the smell of the blood still: all the perfumes of Arabia will / not sweeten this little hand. Oh, oh, oh!
Here's the smell of the blood still. All the perfumes of Arabia won't sweeten this little hand. Oh, oh, oh!
What a sigh is there! The heart is sorely charged.
What a sigh that was! Her heart is heavily burdened.
I would not have such a heart in my bosom for the dignity of the whole / body.
I wouldn't have a heart like that in my breast for all the royal honours of her body.
Pray God it is well, sir.
This disease is beyond my practice: yet I have known those which have / walked in their sleep, who have died holily in their beds.
This illness is beyond my skill. Still, I've known people who walked in their sleep who died peacefully and holily in their beds.
Wash your hands, put on your nightgown; look not so pale. I tell you / yet again, Banquo's buried; he cannot come out on's grave.
Wash your hands. Put on your nightgown. Don't look so pale. I tell you again, Banquo's buried. He can't come out of his grave.
To bed, to bed. There's knocking at the gate. Come, come, come, come, / give me your hand. What's done cannot be undone. To bed, to bed, to / bed.
To bed, to bed. There's knocking at the gate. Come, come, come, come, give me your hand. What's done can't be undone. To bed, to bed, to bed.
Will she go now to bed?
Will she go to bed now?

Foul whisp'rings are abroad. Unnatural deeds / Do breed unnatural troubles: infected minds / To their deaf pillows will discharge their secrets. / More needs she the divine than the physician.— / God, God, forgive us all! Look after her; / Remove from her the means of all annoyance, / And still keep eyes upon her. So, good night: / My mind she has mated, and amaz'd my sight. / I think, but dare not speak.

Evil rumours are going round. Unnatural deeds breed unnatural troubles. Infected minds tell their secrets to their deaf pillows. She needs a priest more than a doctor. God, God forgive us all! Look after her. Take away anything she could hurt herself with, and keep watching her. So, good night. She has confused my mind and amazed my eyes. I have my thoughts, but I don't dare speak them.

The English power is near, led on by Malcolm, / His uncle Siward, and the good Macduff. / Revenges burn in them; for their dear causes / Would to the bleeding and the grim alarm / Excite the mortified man.

The English army is near, led by Malcolm, his uncle Siward and the good Macduff. They're burning for revenge, because their deeply felt causes would rouse even a dead man to the bloody, grim call to battle.
Near Birnam wood / Shall we well meet them. That way are they coming.
We'll meet them near Birnam Wood. That's the way they're coming.
Who knows if Donalbain be with his brother?
Does anyone know if Donalbain is with his brother?
For certain, sir, he is not. I have a file / Of all the gentry: there is Siward's son / And many unrough youths, that even now / Protest their first of manhood.
He certainly isn't, sir. I have a list of all the nobles. Siward's son is there, and many beardless young men who are proving their manhood for the first time.

Great Dunsinane he strongly fortifies. / Some say he's mad; others, that lesser hate him, / Do call it valiant fury: but, for certain, / He cannot buckle his distemper'd cause / Within the belt of rule.
He's strongly fortifying Great Dunsinane. Some say he's mad. Others, who hate him less, call it brave fury. But it's certain that he can't buckle his diseased cause inside the belt of self-control.

Now does he feel / His secret murders sticking on his hands; / Now minutely revolts upbraid his faith-breach; / Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love: now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief.

Now he feels his secret murders sticking to his hands. Now every minute, rebellions condemn his own breach of faith. The men he commands only move because they're ordered to, not out of love. Now he feels his title hanging loose around him, like a giant's robe on a dwarfish thief.
Who, then, shall blame / His pester'd senses to recoil and start, / When all that is within him does condemn / Itself for being there?
Who can blame his tormented senses, then, for jumping and flinching, when everything inside him condemns itself for being there?
Well, march we on, / To give obedience where 'tis truly ow'd: / Meet we the med'cine of the sickly weal; / And with him pour we, in our country's purge, / Each drop of us.
Well, let's march on, to give our obedience where it's truly owed. Let's meet Malcolm, the doctor who will cure our sick country, and pour out every drop of our blood with him to purge it.
Or so much as it needs / To dew the sovereign flower, and drown the weeds. / Make we our march towards Birnam.
Or as much as is needed to water the royal flower and drown the weeds. Let's march towards Birnam.

Bring me no more reports; let them fly all: / Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane / I cannot taint with fear. What's the boy Malcolm? / Was he not born of woman? The spirits that know / All mortal consequences have pronounc'd me thus: / "Fear not, Macbeth; no man that's born of woman / Shall e'er have power upon thee."—Then fly, false thanes, / And mingle with the English epicures: / The mind I sway by, and the heart I bear, / Shall never sag with doubt nor shake with fear.

Don't bring me any more reports. Let them all desert. Until Birnam Wood moves to Dunsinane, I can't be infected with fear. What's the boy Malcolm? Wasn't he born of a woman? The spirits that know all human futures have told me this: "Don't be afraid, Macbeth. No man born of a woman will ever have power over you." So run away, false thanes, and join the soft-living English. The mind I'm ruled by and the heart I carry will never sag with doubt or shake with fear.
The devil damn thee black, thou cream-fac'd loon! / Where gott'st thou that goose look?
May the devil damn you black, you cream-faced fool! Where did you get that stupid goose look?
Go prick thy face and over-red thy fear, / Thou lily-liver'd boy. What soldiers, patch? / Death of thy soul! those linen cheeks of thine / Are counsellors to fear. What soldiers, whey-face?

Go and prick your face and cover your fear with red blood, you coward of a boy. What soldiers, you idiot? Damn your soul! Those white cheeks of yours teach others to be afraid. What soldiers, milk-face?
The English force, so please you.
The English army, if you please.

Seyton!—I am sick at heart, / When I behold—Seyton, I say!—This push / Will cheer me ever or disseat me now. / I have liv'd long enough: my way of life / Is fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf; / And that which should accompany old age, / As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends, / I must not look to have; but, in their stead, / Curses, not loud but deep, mouth-honour, breath, / Which the poor heart would fain deny, and dare not. / Seyton!—

Seyton! I'm sick at heart when I see... Seyton, I said! This attack will either make me secure for ever or throw me off the throne now. I've lived long enough. My life has withered into the dry, yellow leaf of autumn, and the things that should go with old age, like honour, love, obedience and crowds of friends, I can't hope to have. Instead I'll have curses, not loud but deep, and praise from the lips only, empty breath, which the poor heart would like to refuse but doesn't dare. Seyton!
All is confirm'd, my lord, which was reported.
Everything that was reported has been confirmed, my lord.
I'll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack'd. / Give me my armour.
I'll fight until my flesh is hacked off my bones. Give me my armour.
I'll put it on. / Send out more horses, skirr the country round; / Hang those that talk of fear. Give me mine armour.— / How does your patient, doctor?
I'll put it on. Send out more horsemen. Scour the country. Hang anyone who talks of fear. Give me my armour. How is your patient, doctor?
Not so sick, my lord, / As she is troubled with thick-coming fancies, / That keep her from her rest.
She's not so much sick, my lord, as troubled by fantasies crowding in on her, which keep her from resting.

Cure her of that: / Canst thou not minister to a mind diseas'd, / Pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow, / Raze out the written troubles of the brain, / And with some sweet oblivious antidote / Cleanse the stuff'd bosom of that perilous stuff / Which weighs upon the heart?

Cure her of that. Can't you treat a diseased mind, pull a deep-rooted sorrow out of the memory, rub out the troubles written in the brain, and with some sweet drug of forgetfulness clean the clogged heart of the dangerous matter that weighs on it?
Therein the patient / Must minister to himself.
In that, the patient has to treat himself.

Throw physic to the dogs, I'll none of it. / Come, put mine armour on; give me my staff: / Seyton, send out.—Doctor, the Thanes fly from me.— / Come, sir, despatch.—If thou couldst, doctor, cast / The water of my land, find her disease, / And purge it to a sound and pristine health, / I would applaud thee to the very echo, / That should applaud again.—Pull't off, I say.— / What rhubarb, senna, or what purgative drug, / Would scour these English hence? Hear'st thou of them?

Throw medicine to the dogs. I'll have none of it. Come, put my armour on. Give me my lance. Seyton, send out the men. Doctor, the thanes are deserting me. Come, sir, hurry. If you could, doctor, test my country's urine, find out her disease and purge her back to sound, original health, I'd applaud you until the echo applauded back. Pull it off, I said. What rhubarb, senna or other purging drug would flush these English out of here? Have you heard about them?
Ay, my good lord. Your royal preparation / Makes us hear something.
Yes, my good lord. Your royal preparations let us hear something.
Bring it after me.— / I will not be afraid of death and bane, / Till Birnam forest come to Dunsinane.
Bring the armour after me. I won't be afraid of death and destruction until Birnam Forest comes to Dunsinane.
Were I from Dunsinane away and clear, / Profit again should hardly draw me here.
